paras: The attempted lynching of Henry Coleman took place early on September 11, 1888, when a partly masked mob rushed the police station-house in Norfolk, Virginia, to seize Coleman, a Black man held for the murder of a dairyman. Police drove the crowd off, the mayor persuaded it to disperse, and Coleman was moved under military guard to the county jail in Portsmouth. Virginia papers covered the attack at length, including the governor's order that Coleman be protected, while distant papers ran brief notices.

On the afternoon of September 6, James Grant, a dairyman on O'Keefe's farm a few miles from Norfolk, was killed with an axe in his stable, and his housekeeper was attacked and left for dead. Police suspected Coleman, a former driver for Grant who had recently been discharged. Early reports forecast violence: a Savannah paper headed its story "Lynchers on His Heels," and the Richmond Dispatch judged a lynching "probable" if he was caught soon.

Coleman was arrested near Cape Henry on September 10 and brought to the Norfolk jail about 9 p.m., where a crowd of more than three hundred met the officers. According to the Dispatch, he confessed the killing to the sheriff.

At about half-past one the next morning, a mob of young men and boys, some with handkerchiefs over their faces, rushed the entrance of the station-house. The attackers first cut the rope of the alarm bell, but the five policemen on duty beat them back with billies and stood in the doorway with drawn revolvers, firing no shot. Falling back, the crowd smashed the front windows with sticks and stones, and Sergeant Mordecai was hurt by flying glass. Police later collected masks, a sledge hammer and two ropes with slip knots.

Around 2 a.m. Mayor R. G. Banks addressed the rioters, urging them to respect the law and saying it would be "fully vindicated" in Coleman's case. The crowd gave three cheers for the mayor and dispersed, and two of the leaders, Brown and Holland, were captured. At five o'clock Coleman was taken out the rear entrance, handcuffed to two policemen, and carried to the Portsmouth jail with the Norfolk City Guard as escort.

On word that a mob was organizing in Huntersville, Sheriff Bunting had the Old Dominion Guard called out to patrol Portsmouth. Governor Fitzhugh Lee telegraphed that Coleman "must be protected from violence if it takes all the troops" under the regimental commander. Troops stayed at the jail at night through at least September 12, because the sheriff believed the danger of lynching was not over.

James T. Holland and George R. Brown were sent on to court and released on bail of $1,000 each; no report of their trial was found. Coleman was committed for trial after a preliminary examination, and a North Carolina weekly reported that he pleaded guilty and was sent to the October term of the county court. No report of his trial or sentence appears in the coverage.

The Richmond Dispatch gave the fullest account under the headline "A Maddened Mob," crediting the "determined front of the police" and printing the governor's order in full. Its headline placed the attempt "at Portsmouth," though its text described the attack at the Norfolk station-house. The Alexandria Gazette, under "A Mob After a Murderer," described the crowd as "whites and blacks" and put it at about 300, against the Dispatch's seventy-five young men and boys of unstated race.

Both papers called Coleman "the negro" and treated his guilt as settled, with the Dispatch's Norfolk letter calling him "the negro fiend." Elsewhere the attempt ran as a sentence or two in the Washington Evening Star, a Baltimore German daily and an Edenton, North Carolina, weekly, the last reporting that a mob formed to lynch him "but in vain."

The papers differ on the housekeeper, named Read, Reed, Louisa Spratt and Louisa Pratt, and on whether she was stabbed in the neck or struck with the axe. Only a Maryland weekly, which also called the victim "Dr. James Grant," said Coleman had tried to "outrage" a woman; the Norfolk-sourced reports make no such claim.

bases: A crowd, some masked and carrying ropes with slip knots, rushed the Norfolk station-house to take and lynch a jailed prisoner and was driven off by police (A5, A6, A10).
A mob of 75 to 300 tried to seize Coleman, accused of murder, to lynch him, but police repulsed it and he was moved to Portsmouth alive (A5, A6); this was an attempted lynching, not a completed one.

The Richmond Dispatch's special telegram and the separately worded Alexandria Gazette item agree on the masked attack, the police repulse, the mayor's speech, two captures and the transfer to Portsmouth (A5, A6), with briefs in A9, A10 and A14.

framing.detail: The Richmond Dispatch headlined 'A MADDENED MOB', praised the 'determined front of the police', and printed the governor's protection order while calling Coleman 'the negro murderer'.
The Alexandria Gazette's 'A MOB AFTER A MURDERER' stressed the mayor's assurance that 'the law will be fully vindicated'.
Distant papers carried only one- or two-sentence briefs on the attempt.
